summary: Describes a framework for virtual private networks that run across IP backbones, covering the general concepts and requirements. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A VPN is a private tunnel through the public Internet. This is the overview of how to build one.

questions: how do ip based vpns work
what are the types of vpn
what is the difference between vprn and vpls
what is compulsory vs voluntary tunneling
subtitle: A taxonomy of IP-based VPN types and the tunneling, routing and signalling pieces each one needs.

tldr.problem: Virtual private networks over IP backbones were hard to deploy interoperably because there was no agreed definition or scope for what a VPN is, and many different solutions all went by the name.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines a VPN as the emulation of a private WAN using IP facilities, models it like a physical network, and sorts it into four types (virtual leased lines, virtual private routed networks, virtual private dial networks and virtual private LAN segments), listing the requirements and candidate mechanisms for each.
tldr.outcome: It guides later protocol work, such as extensions to IPSec and a VPN membership mechanism, but it is not an IETF working group product and the IETF had no effort underway to standardize a specific VPN framework.

today: RFC 2764 is an Informational memo from February 2000 and, according to its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its IESG note states that it is not the product of an IETF Working Group and that the IETF had no effort underway to standardize a specific VPN framework.

sections.title: What a VPN Is
sections.content:
The document defines a VPN simply as the "emulation of a private Wide Area Network (WAN) facility using IP facilities", including the public Internet or private IP backbones. There are as many types of VPN as there are types of WAN, which explains the confusion over the term.

A VPN is modeled as a connectivity object: hosts attach to it, and VPNs interconnect, in the same way hosts attach to physical networks and physical networks interconnect through bridges or routers. Addressing, forwarding, QoS, security and firewalling all have direct analogues in physical networks, so VPNs do not require reinventing networking. The models are meant to apply to both IPv4 and IPv6 backbones, and VPNs built on native mappings onto switched backbones, such as LAN Emulation or MPOA over ATM, are out of scope. An IESG note says this document is not the product of an IETF Working Group.
sections.eli5: A VPN pretends to be your own private road system, but it is really built from lanes on the big public road network.

sections.title: What Customers Expect
sections.content:
Private networks traditionally come as dedicated WANs (leased lines, Frame Relay or ATM) and dial networks through the PSTN or ISDN. Interest in IP VPNs came from the low cost of Internet service compared with dedicated lines. The memo lists customer requirements:

  • Opaque packet transport: the customer's traffic may be multiprotocol or use private, non-unique IP addressing unrelated to the backbone.
  • Data security: either the customer does not trust the provider and uses CPE devices with secure tunnels, or the customer trusts the provider to supply a secure managed service. Strong mechanisms such as IPSec may be unnecessary inside a single provider backbone but appropriate across several administrations.
  • Quality of service: leased lines offer bandwidth and latency guarantees, and customers will want similar ones from IP VPNs, subject to the capabilities of the underlying backbone.
  • A tunneling mechanism: together the first two requirements imply some form of IP tunneling.

VPNs can be built from customer premises equipment (CPE) or by the ISP in the network. For extranets, where companies share limited data, policy is enforced at interconnection points by firewalls or similar devices, and introducing VPNs does not change that model.
sections.eli5: People who rent a private line want three things: their mail kept secret, their traffic kept separate from everyone else's, and a fast lane when they need it.

sections.title: VPN Tunneling Requirements
sections.content:
An IP tunnel between two VPN endpoints is the basic building block. The IP backbone acts like a link layer and the tunnel is a point-to-point link whose contents are opaque to the backbone. What mainly distinguishes VPN types is how a device forwards packets between interfaces, as a repeater, bridge or router would.

Candidate tunneling mechanisms are IP/IP, GRE, L2TP (RFC 2661), IPSec (RFC 2401) and MPLS. The memo compares them against desirable properties:

  • Multiplexing: L2TP uses tunnel-id and session-id, MPLS uses the label and IPSec uses the SPI. GRE and IP/IP have no true multiplexing field. A VPN-ID format has been standardized (RFC 2685).
  • Signalling: L2TP, IPSec's IKE (RFC 2409) and two MPLS protocols (CR-LDP and RSVP extensions) can set up tunnels dynamically.
  • Data security: only IPSec has intrinsic mechanisms. Its ESP specification precludes an SA with neither encryption nor authentication, but a "null/null" option would be useful for VPNs.
  • Multiprotocol transport: L2TP carries PPP and GRE identifies the protocol, but IP/IP and IPSec assume IP.
  • Frame sequencing: L2TP and GRE have sequence fields. IPSec's sequence number is for anti-replay, not in-order delivery.
  • Maintenance, large MTUs, overhead, flow control and QoS: keepalives, fragmentation inside the tunnel, minimal overhead, and treating a tunnel as a link so existing QoS tools apply.

The recommendation is that IPSec is needed for strong encryption or authentication, and that extending it with a VPN-ID in SA setup, a null/null option, multiprotocol operation and frame sequencing would help. L2TP provides no data security by itself and needs IPSec for strong security.
sections.eli5: A tunnel is a sealed pipe through the public network. The memo checks each kind of pipe for useful features, like labels to tell customers apart or a lock on the pipe.

sections.title: Leased Lines and Routed Networks
sections.content:
Virtual Leased Line (VLL). The simplest type. Two CPE devices are connected by a point-to-point link, for example an ATM virtual circuit at each end, with an IP tunnel between the two ISP nodes. Frames are relayed between the stub link and the tunnel at layer 2, and the payload is opaque to the ISP nodes. The customer may not know part of the circuit runs over IP. The tunnel must support multiprotocol operation and may need sequencing.

Virtual Private Routed Network (VPRN). The emulation of a multi-site routed WAN, where forwarding is done at the network layer. A mesh of IP tunnels joins ISP edge routers, each with a VPN-specific forwarding table, and CPE routers attach over "stub" links. This minimizes CPE configuration: the CPE sees the ISP router as a neighbor and can use a default route. Address spaces may overlap between VPRNs, and TTL is decremented normally, preventing loops.

Building a VPRN requires solving five generic problems: a globally unique VPN identifier, membership determination, stub link reachability, intra-VPRN reachability, and tunnel setup. For each the memo describes options such as directory lookup (for example LDAP), explicit management configuration (MIB or COPS), piggybacking in routing protocols (for example BGP), per-VPRN virtual routers, and link reachability protocols. Full-mesh tunnel topologies are simple and optimal, but the number of tunnels for n sites is n(n-1)/2, which scales poorly. Multicast can be done by edge replication or, with MPLS, native support. Related approaches, including BGP/MPLS VPNs (RFC 2547), fall into piggybacking and virtual routing families.
sections.eli5: A leased line is one private cable between two offices. A routed network joins many offices through the ISP's own routers, and each office only needs to know where to send traffic to the ISP.

sections.title: Dial Networks and LAN Segments
sections.content:
Virtual Private Dial Network (VPDN). Lets a remote user connect on demand through an ad hoc tunnel to a site, with user authentication as the prime requirement. L2TP extends a user's PPP session from an L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC) to an L2TP Network Server (LNS). In compulsory tunneling, a network access server acts as the LAC, transparently to the user. In voluntary tunneling, the tunnel starts on the host itself, using L2TP or IPSec. L2TP over IPSec for voluntary tunnels adds substantial overhead, shown as the stack HTTP/TCP/IP/PPP/L2TP/UDP/ESP/IP/PPP/AHDLC, so using IPSec alone is proposed. IPSec then still needs legacy user authentication and host configuration support, which IKE lacks, and several proposals address this.

Virtual Private LAN Segment (VPLS). Emulates a LAN segment over IP, analogous to LANE over ATM, giving complete protocol transparency. It is modeled as a VPRN where edge nodes bridge at the link layer instead of forwarding at the network layer, so most VPRN mechanisms apply. A VPLS needs broadcast and flooding support. With bridge CPE, scalability is constrained and the scenario suits non-routable protocols. With router CPE, a single subnet joins the routers across the VPLS.

The summary recommends examining IPSec/IKE changes (VPN-ID transport, null/null, multiprotocol, sequencing, legacy user authentication, host configuration), defining modes for IPSec supporting L2TP, defining a directory or MIB based VPN membership mechanism, and keeping solutions applicable across VPN types.
sections.eli5: A dial VPN lets one person phone in and get a private tunnel to the office. A LAN-segment VPN makes far-apart offices feel as if they were plugged into the same wire.
